The current [MATH: I] measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge [MATH: q] measured in coulombs.

[MATH: I = \dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t}]

Differentiating the given expression for [MATH: q(t),] we obtain the following expression for [MATH: I,] in amperes:

[MATH: I(t)|= (d)/(dt)(4e^{− 3t} − 2e^{− t} + (5)/(17)\cos (2t) + (3)/(17)\sin (2t)); = − 12e^{− 3t} + 2e^{− t} − (10)/(17)\sin (2t) + (6)/(17)\cos (2t).]

Note the following:

  • The quantity [MATH: I_c(t) = -12e^{-3t} + 2e^{-t}] is the transient current, since it goes to zero as [MATH: t \to \infty.]

  • The function [MATH: I_p(t) = -\dfrac{10}{17}\sin(2t) + \dfrac{6}{17}\cos(2t)] is the steady-state current. It governs the current's long-term behavior.

Therefore, as [MATH: t\to\infty,] we have [MATH: I(t)\approx I_p(t) = -\dfrac{10}{17}\sin(2t) + \dfrac{6}{17}\cos(2t).]

Finally, the amplitude of the steady-state current, in amperes, is given by [MATH: \sqrt{\left(-\dfrac{10}{17}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{6}{17}\right)^2} = \sqrt{\dfrac{136}{289}} = \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{2\sqrt{34}}{17}}.]

Content:
Suppose we have the following RCL circuit.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/90cca5abccac0c1cf8f6888fb50a7e1c]

Content:
It is possible to write a differential equation that governs the capacitor charge [MATH: q(t)] in a series RCL circuit.

Content:
We know that the voltage drops across the resistor, capacitor, and inductor, respectively, are
[MATH: V_R = RI,
\qquad
V_C = \dfrac{q}{C},
\qquad
V_L = L\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t},]
where [MATH: q(t)] is the charge on the capacitor and [MATH: I(t)] is the circuit current.

Content:
Also, recall that current is the rate at which charge flows, so
[MATH: I = \dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t} = \dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2q}{\mathrm{d}t^2}.]

Content:
Kirchhoff's voltage law states that the source voltage equals the sum of the voltage drops:
[MATH: E = V_R + V_C + V_L]

Content:
So, substituting the expressions above gives an equation in [MATH: q{:}]
[MATH: E = R\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t} + \dfrac{q}{C} + L\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2q}{\mathrm{d}t^2}]

Content:
Finally, dividing both sides by [MATH: L] yields the normalized second-order differential equation governing the charge:
[MATH: \dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2q}{\mathrm{d}t^2} + \dfrac{R}{L}\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t} + \dfrac{1}{LC}\,q = \dfrac{E}{L}]

Content:
To determine a unique solution [MATH: q(t),] we also need initial conditions, typically
[MATH: q(0)=q_0,
\qquad
\left.\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t}\right|_{t=0}=I(0)=I_0.]

The diagram shows a series RCL circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of [MATH: 9\cos(3t)\,\textrm{V},] a resistor of resistance [MATH: 18\,\Omega,] a capacitor of capacitance [MATH: \dfrac1{48}\,\textrm{F},] and an inductor of inductance [MATH: 6\,\textrm{H}.]

The current [MATH: I,] measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge [MATH: q,] measured in coulombs. [MATH: I = \dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t}]

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:
